title: Runecast, a pixel-art autobattler launching Oct 27 — demo is up, and I'll answer anything about our art pipeline
author: Zealousideal-Bar-316
selftext:
First post here, so hi. I'm Nathan, from Brazil. Six of us build games in our spare time and Runecast is the first one we're actually shipping, October 27.



It's an autobattler. You cast runes, three matching runes summon a hero, three identical heroes merge into a higher level. You arrange the formation across three lanes and the fight resolves on its own. Four acts of ten waves, and 16 rune faces you can edit in the forge, so the bag itself ends up being part of the build.



The AI side, since that's what this sub is for. Sprites, backgrounds and audio came out of image/audio generators and PixelLab, working from our own references. None of it went in raw. The game renders at 960x540 and scales at exact integer multiples, so anything not sitting on the pixel grid reads as mush on a 4K monitor. We ended up writing our own pass that crops, scales and snaps every asset to a fixed palette, and that code took longer than generating the art ever did.

All the code, design, balance and writing are ours, and nothing is generated at runtime.

The demo has all of Act 1 plus the Web Queen fight from Act 2, free, English and Portuguese:

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5181900/Runecast\_Demo/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5181900/Runecast_Demo/)



Store page: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5126340/Runecast/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5126340/Runecast/)



If anyone here has a workflow for keeping one character consistent across idle, attack and three evolution tiers without hand-fixing every frame, I'd really like to hear it. That's still the part that fights us.

comments.author: HealthPuzzleheaded
comments.body: can you explain to me the concept of the game? Do you just watch it play itself?

replies.author: Zealousideal-Bar-316
replies.body:
Fair question, and honestly the genre name doesn't help.

You don't control anyone during the fight. What you control is everything that decides it beforehand.

A wave goes like this. You cast runes out of a bag, and three matching runes summon a hero. So you never just pick "I want an archer", you get what the cast gives you and decide what to do with it. Then you place who you got across three lanes, decide who tanks and who stays behind, decide whether to sit on two copies of a hero hoping for the third to merge them into a stronger version or just use them now, and decide which of your finds goes into which of the three slots each hero has. Then you hit go and find out if you were right.

The part that keeps it from being passive: you can edit the 16 rune faces in the forge. So you're not praying for good luck every cast, you're slowly rebuilding the bag so the casts you want become more likely. By the later acts the bag itself is your build.

Closest comparisons are Super Auto Pets and TFT. The fight is the report card, the game is what you did before it. Losing a wave usually points at one specific decision you got wrong, which is the fun part for me.

Demo's free if you want to see it move, it's linked in the post.
